title: Renewal metric specs and KPI checklist
summary: Practical spec & short playbook for measuring the four QBR KPIs we surface in renewal conversations: latency, uptime, cost/token, and cache hit rate — includes measurement queries, thresholds for CS escalations, and a compact KPI table to paste into slide decks.
body:
Purpose and audience:
This is a working spec for Customer Success (renewals + AMs) and the Data/Observability partners. The goal is to standardize how we calculate the four primary QBR metrics we discuss with customers so numbers are comparable quarter-to-quarter and reproducible from telemetry data. Treat this doc as the single source for metric definitions and example queries until we fold into a Confluence canonical page.

Metrics we cover (short):
- Latency (p50 / p95 / cold-start p99): overall request latency measured in ms, from request ingress in front of the inference runtime to first-byte out.
- Uptime (availability): percentage of successful request attempts over total attempts in window (success = non-5xx and response returned).
- Cost per token (USD/token): incremental inference cost divided by tokens generated (customer-billed tokens or internal token counter if unavailable).
- Cache hit rate: fraction of inference requests that are served fully or partially from prefix/KV cache (where caching avoids full forward pass).

Why these four?
They map directly to customer ROI conversations: user-facing latency, reliability, unit economics, and the benefits of caching (cost & latency improvements).

Measurement window and baselines:
- QBR window = last 90 days by default for trend context.
- Compare to prior 90 days for delta; also show 7-day rolling for spikes.
- For newly onboarded customers (<=14 days), use available data and annotate low-volume caveat.

Definitions and calculation recipes (operational):
1) Latency (definitions)
  - p50, p95, p99: percentiles of request-level end-to-end latency (ms). Use server-side ingress timestamp vs first-byte-out for generation starts; for embeddings use end-to-end response time.
  - Cold-start vs warm: define cold-start as requests where backend instance spinup time > 0 (identify from runtime tag "instance_warm=false" or backend_metric 'startup_time_ms' > 0). Report warm p95 separately where possible.
  - Exclude long-tail outliers caused by client-side retries: filter requests with more than 3 upstream retries or where client-retry=true.
  - Example PromQL (conceptual):
    histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="inference"}[7d])) by (le)) * 1000
  - SQL example (from events table):
    SELECT approx_quantile(latency_ms, 0.95) FROM inference_requests WHERE customer_id = 'CUST' AND timestamp BETWEEN X AND Y;

2) Uptime / Availability
  - Definition: uptime = 1 - (failed_requests / total_requests) in window. Failed = 5xx responses or explicit runtime failures (timeout, OOM). 4xx excluded (client errors).
  - Service-level uptime should be presented as a percentage with 3 decimal places for precision (e.g., 99.942%).
  - Alert threshold (CS): if uptime drops below 99.5% for the quarter or below 99.9% in a 7-day window, flag for SRE/AM escalation.
  - Example PromQL:
    1 - (sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5..", customer_id="CUST"}[7d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{customer_id="CUST"}[7d])))

3) Cost per token (methodology)
  - Top-level formula: Cost/token = (inference_cost_allocated + infra_overhead_allocated + caching_savings_adjustment) / generated_tokens.
  - Data inputs: billing export (GPU hours * price), per-model profiling (tokens/sec * GPU utilization), cache reduction estimates. For hosted customers we usually use billing export; for Dedicated use committed pool allocation.
  - Normalize to USD per 1k tokens for readability (USD / 1k tokens).
  - Quick estimate method for QBR (when detailed infra data missing): use model-level cost estimates from model_catalog (e.g., gpt-small-x -> $0.003 / 1k tokens) adjusted by observed avg tokens/session. Mark as "estimate".
  - CS guardrail: call out when cost/token delta > 30% QoQ — requires root-cause analysis (model change, quantization change, token inflation, or billing plan change).

4) Cache hit rate
  - Definition: cache_hit_rate = cached_responses / cache_eligible_requests.
  - cached_responses counts requests fully served from cache plus partial hits (we tally partial separately).
  - cache_eligible_requests: requests where prefix-length >= configured cache_min_prefix AND model supports caching. If instrumentation does not mark eligibility, use heuristic: requests with prompt length > 0 and not streaming-only.
  - Report both overall hit rate and savings-adjusted hit rate (cache_hit_rate * avg_tokens_saved_per_hit / avg_tokens_per_request) so teams can quantify real cost impact.
  - Example query (pseudo):
    SELECT sum(cached_hits) / sum(cache_eligible) FROM cache_metrics WHERE customer_id='CUST' AND ts BETWEEN X AND Y;

KPI table (QBR slide-ready) - pasteable ASCII table
Customer | Metric | Baseline (prior 90d) | Current (90d) | Target | Delta | Notes/Action
-------- | ------ | -------------------- | ------------- | ------ | ----- | -------
Acme Inc | p95 latency | 420 ms | 350 ms | <300 ms | -70 ms | Backend: moved to quantized model q4; investigate further gains
Acme Inc | Uptime | 99.92% | 99.87% | 99.9% | -0.05% | transient region outage in Nov; SRE ticket CS-4522
Acme Inc | Cost / 1k tokens | $2.40 | $1.85 | $1.50 | -$0.55 | cache adoption + smaller model variant
Acme Inc | Cache hit rate | 11% | 28% | 35% | +17% | recommend increasing cache_prefix_threshold to capture more repeats

Suggested thresholds and actions for CS playbook (quick):
- Latency p95 > target: open SRE triage and model-owner review. Short-term: enable burst into dedicated pool or apply traffic shaping. Medium-term: recommend model quantization or a lower-latency variant.
- Uptime < 99.5% (quarter) or < 99.9% (7d): immediate SRE/SE escalation. Communicate customer impact and use fallback model routing if available.
- Cost/token increased > 30% QoQ: dig into model change, prompt inflation, and tokenization differences. Engage Solutions Engineering to suggest batching/quantization/kv cache tuning.
- Cache hit rate < 10% and expected reuse > 20%: recommend customer-side guidance for prompt templates + increase shared-prefix capture in server-side cache.

Instrumentation & queries (practical notes):
- Primary datasources: Redwood Console (aggregates), telemetry exports -> BigQuery, Prometheus (SRE), and billing S3 exports. For QBR slides we pull from BigQuery to ensure reproducible queries.
- Canonical event names: inference_requests, cache_metrics, billing_allocations. Ensure all instrumentation teams add customer_id and model_tag to events.
- Example BigQuery to get tokens and cost: 
  SELECT
    customer_id, SUM(tokens_generated) as tokens, SUM(billed_amount_usd) as cost_usd
  FROM billing_exports.inference_usage
  WHERE customer_id='CUST' AND date BETWEEN X AND Y
  GROUP BY customer_id;

Notes / Known gaps and TODOs:
- We still lack a precise mapping for Dedicated pool internal allocation in some customer billing exports; where missing we tag cost as ESTIMATE and surface assumptions in the QBR.
- Cold-start attribution is noisy; instrumentation work item: add instance_warm boolean to runtime traces (INF-telemetry-233).
- Cache partial-hit accounting: need to standardize "tokens_saved" metric across runtimes (owner: Miguel).

Appendix: quick checklist for AM before QBR slide deck
- Run baseline and current queries (90d) and attach SQL to the QBR ticket.
- Verify customer_id mapping and timezone normalization.
- Annotate anomalies (deployments, model swap, infra incidents) with ticket links.
- If metric is estimation, add a yellow flag row in slide with the estimation method.

Open questions for review (please comment):
- Do we want to report cost/token as USD/1k tokens vs USD/token? Team preference: USD/1k tokens in slides, raw USD/token in telemetry exports.
- Thresholds for cache-hit action — conservative vs aggressive? Proposed above are conservative.
